chapters.title: Chapter 3: Reading a Deal as an Investor

lessons.title: When Acquisitions Destroy Value: Overpaying, Goodwill, and Integration Failure

children.text: In February 2019, Tata Motors reported a consolidated net loss of ₹26,961 crore for the October to December 2018 quarter, then the largest quarterly loss in Indian corporate history. Almost all of it came from a single non-cash line: a write-down of about £3.1 billion on Jaguar Land Rover, the British carmaker it had bought from Ford in 2008. No cash left the company that quarter. The money had been spent years earlier. The impairment was simply the accounting catching up with a value that had not held. Learning to read that trail before the write-down arrives is what this lesson is about.

body.text: Acquisitions destroy value in three ways: paying too much, failing to integrate, and borrowing too heavily to do it. The accounting hides overpayment as goodwill on the balance sheet. Goodwill is the premium still waiting to be proven, and an impairment is the moment the company admits it will not be.

children.text: Where the Premium Goes: Goodwill
When a company buys another, Ind AS 103 requires it to record the target's identifiable assets and liabilities at
fair value
, including intangibles such as brands and customer relationships that never appeared on the target's own balance sheet. Whatever the buyer paid above that is recorded as
goodwill

markDefs.definition: The price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants on the measurement date.
The excess of the purchase price over the fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired. It represents expected synergies, workforce, market position and any overpayment.

body.latex: \text{Goodwill} = \text{Purchase price} - \text{Fair value of identifiable net assets acquired}
body.caption: Simplified for a 100% acquisition. In practice, deferred tax on fair value adjustments and any non-controlling interest also enter the calculation.

children.text: Take the fictional deal from Lesson 3.1: Konkan Paints pays ₹1,800 crore for 100% of Tungabhadra Tiles. Tungabhadra's own balance sheet shows net assets of ₹700 crore. Konkan's valuers then identify assets the old books did not fully capture.

body.title: Calculate the goodwill
body.prompt: Using the purchase price allocation table, how much goodwill does Konkan record on its consolidated balance sheet, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Goodwill = ₹1,800 crore purchase price minus ₹1,050 crore fair value of identifiable net assets = ₹750 crore. Over 40% of the price paid is goodwill: value that exists only if Konkan earns more from Tungabhadra than its identifiable assets alone justify.

body.text: Goodwill is not cash and cannot be sold separately. It is a record of the premium the buyer believed was justified. The larger goodwill is relative to the price paid, the more the deal depends on future performance rather than on assets you can see.

children.text: When the Premium Is Not Earned: Impairment
Under Ind AS, goodwill is not amortised. Instead, under Ind AS 36, it must be tested for
impairment
at least once a year. The company compares the carrying amount of the business unit that holds the goodwill with its
recoverable amount
. If the carrying amount is higher, the difference is written off, starting with goodwill.

markDefs.definition: A write-down of an asset's carrying amount to its recoverable amount when the asset is worth less than the balance sheet says. Impairment losses on goodwill can never be reversed.
The higher of an asset's fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use, which is the present value of the cash flows it is expected to generate.

body.latex: \text{Impairment loss} = \text{Carrying amount of the unit} - \text{Recoverable amount} \quad (\text{if positive})
body.caption: The loss is charged first against goodwill, then against the unit's other assets.

body.title: Three years later
body.prompt: Three years after the deal, a new competitor has cut tile prices. The Tungabhadra business, including its ₹750 crore of goodwill, has a carrying amount of ₹1,900 crore on Konkan's books. Its recoverable amount is now ₹1,400 crore. How much goodwill remains after the impairment, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Impairment loss = ₹1,900 crore minus ₹1,400 crore = ₹500 crore, charged first against goodwill. Goodwill falls from ₹750 crore to ₹250 crore. Konkan's reported profit that year takes a ₹500 crore hit, even though no cash leaves the business.

body.label: Tata Motors, quarter ended 31 December 2018
body.context: Driven by an impairment of about £3.1 billion on Jaguar Land Rover's assets, as weak sales in China, the diesel slump in Europe and Brexit uncertainty cut JLR's expected cash flows.

body.title: What an impairment tells you, and what it does not

columns.label: It tells you
points: Management now expects lower cash flows from the acquired business than it did
Some of the price paid is not expected to be recovered
Return on equity will look better afterwards only because the equity base shrank
The acquisition case deserves a fresh look

columns.label: It does not tell you
points: That cash was lost this quarter: the cash went out when the deal was paid for
That the business is worthless or will not recover: JLR later returned to strong profitability
When the value was actually lost: write-downs often lag reality by years
Whether management will repeat the mistake on the next deal

body.title: Why did the stock barely move?
body.question: A fictional listed company announces a ₹2,000 crore goodwill impairment on a business it bought five years ago. Reported profit turns into a loss for the quarter, but the share price barely moves. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Investors did not notice the loss
The impairment is non-cash and the market had already priced in the weak performance of the acquired business
Impairments increase future cash flows, which offsets the loss
SEBI rules require share prices to ignore exceptional items
body.explanation: Impairments usually confirm what quarterly results have shown for a while. The cash was spent five years ago and the market reprices the business as its earnings disappoint. The write-down matters most as a signal about management's capital allocation, not as fresh bad news.

children.text: The Three Ways Deals Go Wrong
Overpaying.

Bidding wars, peak-cycle prices and optimistic synergy estimates push the premium above what the business can earn back. Tata Steel's contest for Corus in 2007 and Suzlon's fight for control of REpower the same year both ended in prices set by competition, not by cash flows.
Integration failure.

Key people leave, customers drift to competitors during the disruption, IT systems do not talk to each other, and two management cultures clash. Synergies that looked certain in the deal presentation arrive late, or not at all.
Too much debt.

A leveraged acquisition works in good times and becomes dangerous in a downturn. When the acquired business's earnings fall, interest payments do not. A deal that might have survived a bad cycle with equity funding can push a debt-funded buyer into distress.

body.title: Suzlon Energy: acquisitions, debt and distress

events.title: Global expansion by acquisition
events.description: Suzlon buys Belgian gearbox maker Hansen Transmissions and, after a contest with France's Areva, wins control of German turbine maker REpower, funded largely with borrowing and convertible bonds.

events.title: Global financial crisis
events.description: Wind turbine orders slow and credit tightens just as Suzlon's debt burden peaks.

events.title: Default on foreign currency convertible bonds
events.description: Suzlon fails to repay maturing FCCBs and enters corporate debt restructuring with its Indian lenders.

events.title: REpower, renamed Senvion, is sold
events.description: Suzlon sells the business to raise money to reduce debt. Shareholders who bought during the expansion years suffered a long, deep decline.

children.text: Spotting Trouble Before the Write-Down
The clearest early warning is falling
return on capital employed

. An acquisition adds the full purchase price to capital employed on day one, but the acquired profits must justify it. Before the deal, Konkan earned EBIT of ₹700 crore on capital employed of ₹2,900 crore. Tungabhadra adds ₹140 crore of EBIT, while the ₹1,800 crore price, funded by debt, adds the same amount to capital employed.

markDefs.definition: ROCE. Earnings before interest and tax divided by capital employed (equity plus debt). It shows how much operating profit a company generates for every rupee invested in it.

body.title: Konkan Paints ROCE before and after the acquisition

children.text: Before: ₹700 crore ÷ ₹2,900 crore = 24.1%. After: (₹700 crore + ₹140 crore) ÷ (₹2,900 crore + ₹1,800 crore) = ₹840 crore ÷ ₹4,700 crore = 17.9%. Tungabhadra itself earns only ₹140 crore on ₹1,800 crore paid, or 7.8%, far below Konkan's existing business. Unless synergies close that gap, every year the deal drags down the return Konkan earns on its shareholders' money.

body.title: The balance sheet footprint
body.textWithBlank: The excess of the purchase price over the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired is recorded on the balance sheet as ___.
body.explanation: Goodwill sits in intangible assets on the consolidated balance sheet. Under Ind AS it is tested for impairment every year rather than amortised.

body.title: Why older Indian accounts treated goodwill differently

children.text: Before Ind AS became mandatory for large companies from 2016 onwards, most Indian companies followed Indian GAAP. Under AS 14, goodwill arising on an amalgamation was normally amortised over a period not exceeding five years, so it gradually disappeared from the balance sheet regardless of how the business performed.

Under Ind AS 103 and Ind AS 36, goodwill stays at cost until an impairment test shows otherwise. That makes goodwill on today's balance sheets a more visible record of past deal premiums, but it also means a bad deal can sit unimpaired for years if management's cash flow forecasts stay optimistic. Read the impairment testing note, which discloses the growth and discount rates used.

body.title: The serial acquirer
body.scenario: A fictional listed mid-cap, Vindhya Specialty, has made seven acquisitions in five years. Revenue has tripled and management calls itself a "platform consolidator". On screener.in you see ROCE fall from 22% to 11%, borrowings rise from ₹300 crore to ₹2,400 crore, and cumulative operating cash flow over the five years equal to only about half of cumulative EBITDA. Goodwill is now 55% of net worth. The stock is up 40% this year on a new acquisition announcement.
body.prompt: What is this data telling you, and what would you want to see before trusting the growth story?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Revenue growth has been bought, not earned. Tripling revenue while ROCE halves means the acquired businesses are earning far less than Vindhya paid for them.
2. Cash conversion is weak. Operating cash flow at about half of EBITDA suggests working capital build-up, aggressive revenue recognition or integration costs that are not visible in profits.
3. Leverage is climbing. Borrowings up eight times make the company vulnerable if any acquired business stumbles or rates rise.
4. Goodwill at 55% of net worth means more than half the equity depends on past deal premiums being justified. A few impairments could wipe out a large part of book value.
5. Before trusting the story, look for: organic growth disclosed separately from acquired growth, ROCE of each acquired business, the impairment testing note with its growth and discount assumptions, and whether management's pay is linked to revenue size or to returns.
6. The 40% rally tells you the market is rewarding the announcement, not the track record.

body.title: Post-acquisition health check
steps: Track ROCE for three years after the deal against the acquirer's pre-deal ROCE
Compare goodwill with net worth and note any change each year
Check that operating cash flow keeps pace with EBITDA
Watch exceptional items and integration costs in the profit and loss statement
Read the impairment testing note for growth and discount rate assumptions
Compare the synergies promised at announcement with what management reports later

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Open any acquirer's page and look at ten years of ROCE, borrowings and cash from operations to see whether its acquisitions have paid off.

cards.definition: Purchase price minus the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired.
The process of assigning the price paid to the target's identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, with the remainder recorded as goodwill.
A write-down when an asset's carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount. Goodwill impairments cannot be reversed.
The higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use.
The Indian accounting standard on business combinations, which requires fair value accounting and recognition of goodwill.
The Indian accounting standard on impairment of assets, requiring goodwill to be tested at least annually.
EBIT divided by capital employed. A falling ROCE after acquisitions is an early sign of overpayment.

points: Acquisitions destroy value through overpaying, integration failure and excessive debt, often all three together.
Goodwill is the purchase price minus the fair value of identifiable net assets. It is the premium still waiting to be justified.
Under Ind AS, goodwill is tested for impairment at least annually rather than amortised, and write-downs cannot be reversed.
Impairments are non-cash and usually late: Tata Motors' ₹26,961 crore quarterly loss in 2018 recognised value lost on JLR over earlier years.
Falling ROCE, weak cash conversion, rising debt and goodwill growing as a share of net worth are signs of trouble long before any write-down.
Suzlon shows how debt-funded acquisitions at the top of a cycle can turn a growth story into years of distress.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or accounting advice. Konkan Paints, Tungabhadra Tiles and Vindhya Specialty are fictional. Accounting treatment is simplified, and actual purchase price allocations and impairment tests involve more detail, including deferred taxes. Figures and events for Tata Motors, Tata Steel and Suzlon are from public disclosures and news reports. Mentioning a company is not a recommendation to buy or sell its shares.
